Microsoft Edge — Microsoft introduced Edge with Windows 10 and later rebuilt it on Chromium.
DuckDuckGo — DuckDuckGo markets its service around reduced tracking and private searching.

at sign — Ray Tomlinson chose @ to separate the mailbox name from the host computer.

Facebook — The service began as a college network created by Mark Zuckerberg and fellow students.
YouTube — YouTube developed into a major video-sharing platform and was acquired by Google in 2006.
Twitter — Twitter popularised a public stream of brief messages and the use of hashtags.
LinkedIn — Members build résumé-like profiles and connect with colleagues, employers, and clients.

touchscreen — A touchscreen combines visual output with a sensor that locates contact on its surface.

Android — Android is an open-source mobile platform developed through Google and the Open Handset Alliance.

Skype — Skype was developed with important Estonian engineering work and launched in 2003.
WhatsApp — WhatsApp supports text, voice, video, and file sharing between registered phone numbers.
Spotify — Spotify launched as an on-demand audio streaming service in 2008.
Google Maps — Google Maps combines mapping, place information, satellite imagery, and navigation.
Shazam — Shazam creates an acoustic fingerprint and compares it with a database of recorded music.
pixel — A raster image is a grid of pixels, each carrying colour or brightness information.
megapixel — Camera resolution is often described by the number of millions of sensor pixels.
memory card — Cameras commonly write image files to formats such as SD cards.
image sensor — A digital camera focuses light onto a sensor made of many light-sensitive sites.
optical zoom — Optical zoom magnifies the scene before it reaches the sensor and therefore preserves captured detail.
headphones — Headphones place small loudspeaker drivers close to each ear.
loudspeaker — A loudspeaker moves a diaphragm to create pressure waves in the surrounding air.
stereo — Stereophonic sound presents related but different signals through two channels.
audio amplifier — An audio power amplifier raises signal power to a level suitable for a speaker or headphones.
active noise cancellation — The system measures ambient sound and plays a waveform intended to cancel part of it.
remote control — A television remote normally sends coded infrared or radio signals to the receiver.
LCD — A liquid-crystal display modulates a backlight or reflected light at each pixel.
OLED — Each OLED subpixel produces light directly, so a separate backlight is unnecessary.
HDMI — High-Definition Multimedia Interface carries uncompressed digital video together with audio.
set-top box — A set-top box converts broadcast, cable, satellite, or internet signals into television output.
FM — Frequency modulation represents the audio signal through small changes in carrier frequency.
antenna — An antenna converts guided electrical energy to radio waves or performs the reverse conversion.
AM — Amplitude modulation changes signal strength in step with the audio waveform.
tuner — The tuner filters and converts the chosen channel so its programme can be recovered.

refrigerator — A refrigerator moves heat from an insulated interior to the surrounding room.
vacuum cleaner — A fan creates lower pressure so air carries dirt away from floors and furniture.
microwave oven — Microwaves make polar molecules, especially water, rotate and generate heat in food.
dishwasher — A dishwasher circulates wash water around plates, cups, and cutlery before rinsing them.
induction cooktop — An induction hob creates an alternating magnetic field that induces electric currents in ferromagnetic cookware.
bicycle — A rider turns pedals that drive the rear wheel, usually through a chain.
steam locomotive — The boiler supplies pressurised steam to cylinders connected to the driving wheels.
internal-combustion engine — Combustion gases expand inside the engine and push pistons or a turbine.
jet engine — A jet engine draws in air, compresses it, adds fuel, and expels hot gas rearward.
hovercraft — Fans force air beneath the craft, while a flexible skirt helps retain the supporting cushion.
stethoscope — The instrument carries acoustic vibrations from a chest piece to the listener’s ears.
MRI — Magnetic resonance imaging measures signals from atomic nuclei aligned in a magnetic field.
pacemaker — An artificial pacemaker stimulates heart muscle when its natural electrical rhythm is inadequate.
defibrillator — Defibrillation sends a controlled electrical pulse through the heart during certain life-threatening arrhythmias.
insulin pump — An insulin pump supplies rapid-acting insulin throughout the day and can add doses around meals.
printing press — A press produces repeated impressions more quickly and consistently than hand copying.
e-book — An electronic book packages text and images as a digital publication.

movable type — Printers arrange separate pieces of type, print a run, and redistribute them for later pages.
typesetting — Typesetting controls typeface, spacing, line breaks, and page composition.

Samuel Morse — Morse and Alfred Vail developed an electrical telegraph system and its signalling code.

Steve Jobs — Steve Jobs co-founded Apple and was central to several of its best-known personal technology products.
bug — A software bug is a flaw in code, design, or requirements that causes unintended behaviour.
algorithm — An algorithm gives finite, unambiguous instructions that transform input into an intended result.
variable — A variable associates an identifier with data during program execution.
loop — A loop continues for a set count or while a condition remains true.
compiler — A compiler processes a program before execution and emits target code or an intermediate representation.

phishing — Phishing impersonates a trusted sender and directs victims toward fraudulent requests.
firewall — A firewall examines traffic crossing a network boundary and enforces an access policy.
encryption — Encryption applies a cipher and key to produce ciphertext from plaintext.
two-factor authentication — Two-factor authentication combines factors from separate categories so one stolen credential is insufficient.
backup — A backup preserves data on another medium or service so the original can be restored.
password manager — A password manager keeps credentials in an encrypted vault and can generate unique passwords.
software update — Updates often patch security vulnerabilities as well as correcting functional defects.
privacy settings — Privacy controls restrict the audience for profile information and shared content.
digital footprint — Posts, searches, accounts, and collected metadata all contribute to an online trace.
sensor — Sensors convert physical conditions into signals a control system can process.
humanoid robot — Humanoid designs commonly use a torso, head, arms, and sometimes two legs.
industrial robot — Industrial robots repeat precise motions and can carry tools or parts through several axes.
robot vacuum cleaner — A robotic vacuum cleaner uses sensors and motors to clean floors with limited human direction.
autonomous robot — Autonomous robots combine sensing, decision-making, and action to operate independently for a period.
satellite — Artificial satellites circle Earth or another body and carry instruments for a defined mission.
spacesuit — A spacesuit functions as a personal spacecraft, maintaining a breathable pressurised environment.

rover — A rover carries instruments across terrain beyond the immediate landing site.
launch vehicle — A launch vehicle produces thrust in stages to accelerate a payload toward its required trajectory.
solar panel — Photovoltaic cells in a panel generate electricity when light strikes semiconductor material.

wind turbine — Wind turns rotor blades connected through a drive train to an electrical generator.
electric vehicle — Electric vehicles use one or more traction motors powered from batteries, fuel cells, or an external supply.
green hydrogen — Green hydrogen production splits water with electricity from renewable sources, avoiding fossil fuel as the energy input.

Java — Java was named after coffee, and a steaming cup became its familiar logo.

Bubble wrap — Its inventors sealed air bubbles between plastic sheets while experimenting with wallpaper.
Slinky — Richard James noticed that a dropped spring stepped through a series of arcs instead of simply falling.
Ice pop — Frank Epperson later developed his accidentally frozen drink into the ice pop sold as the Popsicle.
Super Glue — Cyanoacrylate was encountered during materials research and later marketed as Super Glue.
Umbrella — An umbrella spreads a fabric canopy over folding ribs to shelter its user.
Eyeglasses — Eyeglasses hold lenses that correct or protect a wearer’s vision.

function key — Its purpose depends on the program, and it belongs to the numbered F row.

numeric keypad — It provides a calculator-style arrangement for entering numbers quickly.

teletext — Teletext sends numbered pages of text and simple graphics within a television broadcast signal for equipped sets.

portal gun — The Aperture Science Handheld Portal Device creates a linked pair of openings that players and objects can pass through.

neoprene — Foamed neoprene insulates wetsuits by holding water and tiny gas bubbles close to the wearer's body.
elastane — Elastane, Spandex, and the Lycra brand all refer to the highly elastic synthetic fibre used in close-fitting clothing.

typewriter — A mechanical typewriter prints characters through an inked ribbon and moves its carriage across the page one position at a time.
photocopier — A xerographic photocopier uses light, electrostatic charge, a photoconductive drum, and toner to reproduce documents.

carbon paper — Carbon paper carried pigment to a second sheet under pressure, creating the carbon copy abbreviated as CC.

fingerprint scanner — A fingerprint scanner captures distinctive ridge features and compares them with an enrolled digital template.

grade separation — Grade separation uses bridges or tunnels to keep crossing traffic streams at different levels.
runway — A runway is the defined rectangular area at an airport prepared for aircraft landing and takeoff.
baggage carousel — A baggage carousel is a conveyor system that delivers checked luggage to passengers in an arrivals area.
jet bridge — A jet bridge is a movable enclosed connector that lets passengers board an aircraft directly from the terminal.
control tower — A control tower houses airport controllers who manage aircraft on runways and nearby airspace.
air traffic control — Air traffic control coordinates aircraft on the ground and in controlled airspace to keep traffic safe and orderly.
conveyor belt — A conveyor belt uses a moving belt to carry materials or goods from one place to another.
forklift truck — A forklift truck lifts and moves loads with forked arms, especially on pallets.
pallet — A pallet is a flat transport structure that supports goods while they are lifted and moved.
parcel locker — A parcel locker has secure compartments where delivery companies leave packages for collection.
RFID — RFID identifies tagged objects by radio waves, so the tag does not need a visible optical code.
cash register — A cash register records sales and commonly includes a drawer for cash and a receipt printer.
chip card — A chip card contains an integrated circuit that can store data and take part in secure transactions.
online banking — Online banking provides banking services through the internet instead of only at a branch.
point-of-sale terminal — A point-of-sale terminal is the checkout device used to process card payments.
payment gateway — A payment gateway securely transmits payment information between an online merchant and payment processors.
CAPTCHA — A CAPTCHA is designed to distinguish people from automated programs on a website.
spam filter — A spam filter identifies unwanted email and separates it from ordinary inbox messages.
private browsing — Private browsing prevents a browser from retaining local history and session data after the private windows are closed.
virtual private network — A virtual private network extends a private network across a public network through an encrypted connection.
HTTPS — HTTPS is HTTP used over an encrypted connection, helping protect data exchanged with a website.
speech recognition — Speech recognition uses software to identify spoken words or commands.
text-to-speech — Text-to-speech converts written text into spoken audio produced by a computer.
screen reader — A screen reader presents screen content through speech or other non-visual output.
machine translation — Machine translation uses software to translate text or speech from one language into another.
natural language processing — Natural language processing is the field concerned with computer processing of human language.
excavator — An excavator uses a boom, stick, and bucket to dig and move earth.
bulldozer — A bulldozer is a powerful tracked vehicle with a large front blade for pushing material.
concrete mixer — A concrete mixer combines cement, water, and aggregate to make concrete.
tower crane — A tower crane is a tall crane used to lift heavy materials to great heights on construction sites.
tunnel boring machine — A tunnel boring machine excavates circular tunnels through soil or rock with a rotating cutting head.
email — Email routes messages through networked mail systems, with the domain naming the receiving server.
video conference — A video conference carries live audio and video between participants in different locations.
instant messaging — Instant messaging can deliver short text almost immediately and stores messages for recipients who are temporarily offline.
emoji — Emoji are pictographic characters used in electronic messages; the word comes from Japanese e and moji.
teleprinter — A teleprinter combined a typewriter with telegraphy and was widely used by newsrooms and railways.
windsock — A windsock's narrow end streams downwind, opposite the direction the wind comes from. Its angle and extension give a visual wind check before take-off or landing.
aircraft de-icing — Ice changes an aircraft wing’s shape and can seriously reduce lift, so it must be removed before flight.
runway lighting — Runway lighting gives pilots visual information for locating and aligning with a runway at night or in poor visibility.
black box — The popular name covers flight-data and cockpit-voice recorders, which are painted orange to make recovery easier.
wind tunnel — A wind tunnel produces controlled airflow around a model so engineers can measure aerodynamic forces.
power station — A power station uses generators, often driven by turbines, to supply electricity to a grid.
fuse — A fuse protects a circuit by melting its metal element when current exceeds a safe level.
electric motor — An electric motor uses the force between magnetic fields and electric current to produce rotation, making it the moving part in countless appliances and vehicles.
electric generator — A generator makes electricity by moving a conductor through a magnetic field. Wind turbines supply the rotation; the generator supplies the electrical output.
power inverter — A power inverter performs DC-to-AC conversion. It lets battery-based or solar systems run equipment designed for an AC wall outlet.
Brooklyn Bridge — Completed in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge spans the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn. Its stone towers and suspension cables made it an early engineering landmark.
Hoover Dam — Hoover Dam controls the Colorado River at Black Canyon and created Lake Mead. Its construction in the 1930s also supplied flood control and hydroelectric power.

Trans-Alaska Pipeline System — The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System carries North Slope oil almost 1,300 kilometres to Valdez. Much of it is elevated so heat from the oil does not thaw the permafrost below.
Delta Works — The Delta Works are a connected Dutch flood-defence system. Their dams and movable barriers shorten the exposed coastline and can close during dangerous storm surges.
Gotthard Base Tunnel — The Gotthard Base Tunnel is a flat, low-level route through the Alps. It was designed to move freight and passenger trains more efficiently than the older mountain line.
rubber band — A rubber band is an elastic loop whose stretched rubber returns toward its original shape. That elastic force keeps a bundle together without a permanent fastening.
tape measure — A measuring tape is a flexible graduated ruler, commonly a metal strip that coils into a protective case. Its sliding hook makes inside and outside measurements practical.
can opener — A can opener uses a sharp cutting wheel and a gripping wheel to travel around a can's rim. This opened canned food without requiring a knife or puncturing by hand.
corkscrew — A corkscrew's pointed helix bites into the cork, giving the user a grip for extraction. Lever designs add mechanical advantage to make the pull easier.

safety match — A safety match separates reactive chemicals between the match head and its prepared striking surface. The Swedish design used red phosphorus on the surface, reducing accidental ignition.
Wi-Fi — Wi-Fi is a family of wireless local-network standards. A router uses radio signals to connect nearby devices to the local network and often to the internet.
airplane mode — Airplane mode disables a device’s cellular radio transmission for air travel. Wi-Fi or Bluetooth can often be switched back on separately when the airline allows it.
URL shortener — A URL shortener maps a short address to a longer destination and redirects the visitor. This makes unwieldy links easier to distribute, though the destination can be hidden.
inductive charging — Inductive charging uses coils to create and receive a changing magnetic field. The energy crosses the small air gap without an exposed cable connection.
RSS feed — An RSS feed is a machine-readable list of recent website updates. Feed-reader software can collect subscriptions from many sites in one place.
monorail — A monorail uses one guiding rail rather than the two rails of conventional track. Systems can be straddle-beam or suspended beneath the beam.
snowmobile — A snowmobile steers with front skis while a powered rubber track drives it over snow. The wide track spreads its weight so it does not sink as readily.
maglev — Maglev trains use magnetic forces for levitation, guidance, and propulsion. With no wheel-on-rail contact at speed, they avoid the rolling friction of ordinary trains.
aerial tramway — An aerial tramway suspends one or more passenger cabins from cables stretched between stations. Unlike a funicular, its cabins travel through the air rather than on rails.
funicular — A funicular uses two rail cars linked by a cable on a steep slope. Their opposing movement helps counterbalance the load and reduces the power needed.
digital camera — A digital camera uses an electronic image sensor instead of film. The sensor converts light into digital data that can be stored, edited, and shared.
telescope — A telescope uses lenses or mirrors to collect more light than the eye alone and form a magnified view of a distant object.
microscope — A microscope combines lenses to form a magnified image of a small specimen. Light microscopes are commonly used to study cells and other tiny structures.
radar — Radar determines an object's range from the time a radio pulse takes to return as an echo. It is used for navigation, weather observation, and air-traffic control.
thermal imaging — Thermal imaging detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and maps it to a visible image. It can reveal heat loss from buildings, warm machinery, or people in darkness.
flip book — A flip book presents slightly changed pictures in rapid succession, creating the illusion of motion when the pages are thumbed through.
hologram — A hologram records both intensity and phase information in light, so it can reproduce a view that changes with the observer's angle rather than a flat photograph.
animatronics — Animatronics combines mechanical structures, motors, electronics, and controls to make a figure move. It is widely used for characters in themed entertainment.
zoetrope — A zoetrope is a slotted rotating cylinder containing a sequence of pictures. Looking through the slits separates the images enough for them to appear to move.
cinematograph — The Cinématographe was a compact machine that could act as a camera, film processor, and projector. The Lumière brothers used it for landmark public film screenings in 1895.
heat pump — A heat pump transfers thermal energy using a refrigerant cycle. Because it moves existing heat, it can supply more heat indoors than the electrical energy it consumes.
hydroelectricity — Hydroelectricity is generated when moving water drives a turbine connected to a generator. A dam can store water and release it through turbines when power is needed.
nuclear reactor — In a nuclear reactor, a controlled fission chain reaction produces heat. Nuclear power stations commonly use that heat to make steam that drives turbine generators.
geothermal energy — Geothermal energy comes from heat inside the Earth. In volcanic regions such as Iceland, hot water and steam can be used for district heating and electricity generation.
biogas — Biogas is formed by anaerobic digestion, in which microorganisms break down organic matter without oxygen. Its methane content lets it be burned for heat or electricity.
3D printer — A 3D printer is an additive-manufacturing machine: it creates an object by adding material in successive layers from a digital model.
laser cutter — Laser cutting directs a high-power focused beam at a material to melt, burn, or vaporise a narrow path. Computer control makes complex repeatable cuts possible.
CNC machine — A CNC machine follows a programmed sequence of numerical coordinates to control tools precisely. The same code can reproduce matching parts again and again.
injection moulding — Injection moulding fills a closed mould with molten material under pressure and then cools it. It is especially efficient when a factory needs many identical plastic components.
lathe — A lathe holds and turns a workpiece while a cutting tool removes material. It is one of the fundamental machine tools for making round or threaded parts.
Tacoma Narrows Bridge — The bridge’s failure became a classic warning that wind-induced motion must be considered in suspension-bridge design.
Mars Climate Orbiter — The loss highlighted the practical importance of unit consistency and interface checks in complex engineering projects.
de Havilland Comet — Investigators linked the early Comet crashes to fatigue cracks, prompting redesigned windows and stronger fatigue testing.
Hyatt Regency walkway collapse — The disaster made design-change review and clear responsibility between engineers, fabricators, and contractors central safety lessons.
Ariane 5 — The 1996 failure is a well-known case in which software proven on an earlier rocket was unsafe under the new vehicle’s conditions.
dynamite — Kieselguhr stabilized the nitroglycerin into a portable explosive that Nobel named dynamite.
Gorilla Glass — Corning revived its chemically strengthened glass work for consumer electronics, and the first iPhone shipped with glass later branded Gorilla Glass.
Vaseline — Chesebrough refined the oil-pump residue into petroleum jelly and began manufacturing it under the name Vaseline.
Silly Putty — The bouncy silicone material did not replace rubber, but marketer Peter Hodgson turned it into the egg-packaged toy Silly Putty.
mauveine — Perkin's failed quinine experiment yielded mauveine, one of the first synthetic dyes to be mass-produced.
Jacquard loom — The Jacquard loom encoded each textile pattern on cards, an idea Charles Babbage later drew on for the Analytical Engine.
Colossus — Colossus was programmable by switches and plugs and is regarded as one of the first electronic digital computers.
UNIVAC I — UNIVAC I was the first general-purpose electronic digital computer designed for business use in the United States.
Xerox Alto — The Alto was developed at Xerox PARC, where its graphical interface, mouse, Ethernet networking, and printer services influenced later personal-computer design.
IBM System/360 — System/360 made compatibility across a product line a defining commercial idea, despite a costly and risky development programme.
Netscape Navigator — Netscape Navigator rapidly gained web-browser market share before Internet Explorer displaced it in the late 1990s.
Mosaic — Mosaic’s accessible graphical interface helped carry the web beyond specialist academic users in the early 1990s.
VisiCalc — VisiCalc let users recalculate linked financial figures on a personal computer, creating demand for the Apple II in offices.
Lotus 1-2-3 — Lotus 1-2-3 became the leading spreadsheet package for IBM-compatible PCs during the 1980s.
WordStar — WordStar’s keyboard commands made it an influential writing tool before graphical word processors became standard.
ICQ — ICQ popularised presence indicators and direct online messaging for a large international audience.
Napster — Napster connected users who shared music files directly and its lawsuits helped shape later digital-music services.
GeoCities — GeoCities gave non-specialists tools and space to publish personal pages, before it was closed in 2009.
bulletin board system — Bulletin board systems, usually called BBSes, let callers exchange messages and files before the web became widespread.
Usenet — Usenet passed articles between servers, creating public discussion groups that influenced later online forums.
Leica I — The Leica I developed from Oskar Barnack’s small-format design and encouraged portable, candid photography.
Kodachrome — Kodachrome was a subtractive colour-reversal process whose distinctive look made it an important film stock for decades.
daguerreotype — Louis Daguerre’s process was publicly announced in 1839 and made detailed photographic portraits possible.
Brownie camera — The Brownie was simple and cheap enough to bring photography to a mass market rather than trained professionals alone.
dry plate — Dry plates made cameras more portable because photographers no longer had to prepare and develop a plate while it was still wet.
Deepsea Challenger — Deepsea Challenger was built for an extremely deep solo dive and collected scientific samples and images from the ocean floor.
Trieste — Trieste reached the Mariana Trench's deepest known point, demonstrating that people could descend to the ocean’s greatest depth.
Alvin — Alvin is a crewed deep-ocean research vehicle operated for scientific work by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.
bathysphere — The Bathysphere had no propulsion of its own; a surface ship lowered and raised it by cable.
SEALAB — SEALAB placed experimental habitats on the sea floor and helped develop knowledge about saturation diving.
Panama Canal locks — The canal’s lock chambers use gravity-fed water to lift ships over the continental divide and lower them again.
Thames Barrier — The Thames Barrier has movable gates that can be raised to stop a surge travelling upstream toward London.
Akashi Kaikyō Bridge — The bridge crosses the Akashi Strait, a route exposed to strong winds, tides, and earthquakes.
Lærdal Tunnel — The Lærdal Tunnel was designed with large, lit caverns to reduce monotony and help drivers stay alert on the long journey.
Maeslantkering — Maeslantkering is part of the Netherlands' Delta Works and closes the Nieuwe Waterweg to protect the Rotterdam region from storm surges.
Voyager 1 — Voyager 1 launched in 1977, made landmark outer-planet observations, and later crossed the heliopause into interstellar space.
Explorer 1 — Explorer 1 was launched in 1958 and its observations led to the identification of radiation belts around Earth.
Luna 2 — Luna 2 impacted the lunar surface in 1959 and was the first spacecraft to reach another celestial body.
Pioneer 10 — Pioneer 10 passed Jupiter in 1973 and was the first spacecraft to travel through the asteroid belt.
Mariner 2 — Mariner 2 flew past Venus in 1962 and returned measurements that changed early ideas about the planet’s environment.
Commodore 64 — The Commodore 64 combined low price, 64 KB of RAM, colourful graphics, and the SID sound chip, helping it become one of the best-selling computers ever.
ZX Spectrum — The ZX Spectrum's low price and recognisable rubber-key model helped create a large market for British home-computer games.
Amiga 500 — The Amiga 500 made the Amiga platform broadly popular in a compact home-computer case, with dedicated chips for graphics and sound.
Altair 8800 — MITS sold the Altair 8800 as a kit; its January 1975 Popular Electronics cover story drew hobbyists who soon formed clubs and wrote software for it.
TRS-80 — The TRS-80 Model I was sold through Radio Shack stores as a complete system, unlike many hobby kits of the period.
Hubble Space Telescope — Hubble's position above the atmosphere lets it make sharp observations, and its servicing missions corrected its early mirror problem.
Landsat 1 — Landsat 1, first called ERTS-1, supplied multispectral images of Earth and established the Landsat remote-sensing programme.
Telstar 1 — Telstar 1 was an active communications satellite in a low orbit, so its transatlantic relay windows were brief but historic.
TIROS-1 — TIROS-1 was the first successful low-Earth-orbit weather satellite and returned images that revealed cloud systems on a large scale.
Syncom 3 — Syncom 3 stayed over one point on the equator, a practical breakthrough for continuous communications and Olympic television coverage.
inkjet printer — Inkjet printers propel fine droplets. Continuous systems form a stream and recycle unused drops, while drop-on-demand systems expel individual drops as needed.
laser printer — A laser printer uses a focused beam swept by a rotating mirror to write an electrostatic image on a drum; toner follows that image and is fused to paper with heat.
direct thermal printer — Direct thermal printing darkens a heat-sensitive coating; laminator heat can therefore turn an entire sonogram black, while light can later fade the image.
dot-matrix printer — Dot-matrix printers use impact pins, so they can press through carbon copies even though their output is coarse and noisy.
plotter — A plotter makes vector-style line drawings by moving a pen, or later a cutting or printing tool, with computer-controlled precision.
smoke detector — Smoke detectors normally sense airborne smoke particles, either optically or through ionisation, and trigger an alarm.
fire sprinkler system — A sprinkler system normally activates only heads heated by the fire, delivering water where it is needed first.
crash test dummy — Crash-test dummies carry sensors that record the loads a body would experience, helping designers compare restraint and vehicle designs.
seat belt pretensioner — A seat-belt pretensioner removes slack almost instantly during a crash, helping the belt restrain the occupant sooner and reducing forward movement.
Jaws of Life — Jaws of Life is a widely used name for hydraulic rescue tools that cut, spread, or ram apart vehicle structure after a crash.
Concorde — Concorde was a supersonic airliner jointly developed by Britain and France; its speed made transatlantic journeys notably shorter.
Montgolfier balloon — The Montgolfiers demonstrated that heated air could lift a large balloon, and the first free human flight followed later in 1783.
Graf Zeppelin — Graf Zeppelin carried passengers on long-distance flights and completed a widely publicised circumnavigation in 1929.
Bell X-1 — The Bell X-1 was designed for high-speed research and became the first piloted aircraft confirmed to exceed Mach 1 in level flight.
Solar Impulse 2 — Solar Impulse 2 combined solar cells, large batteries, and extreme lightness to complete its 2015–2016 circumnavigation without fuel.
Plexiglas — Plexiglas is a brand of polymethyl methacrylate, a transparent plastic used where glass would be heavy or fragile.
Kevlar — Kevlar is an aramid synthetic fibre with high tensile strength relative to its weight, allowing tough protective fabrics without much bulk.
Styrofoam — Styrofoam is DuPont's trademark for extruded polystyrene foam; in the United States, everyday use of the word often covers other foamed polystyrene packaging.
Mylar — Mylar is a brand name for biaxially oriented PET film, valued for strength, electrical insulation, and a reflective metallised form.
Formica — Formica is a high-pressure decorative laminate; its name came from its original use as a replacement for mica in electrical insulation.
slide rule — A slide rule uses logarithmic scales, turning multiplication and division into addition and subtraction of distances.
Pascaline — The Pascaline used numbered wheels and a carrying mechanism to perform addition and subtraction mechanically.
arithmometer — The arithmometer was the first mass-produced mechanical calculator and made the four basic arithmetic operations practical in offices.
Comptometer — The Comptometer's many keys directly engaged its mechanism, making fast repetitive calculations possible for office workers.
Curta calculator — The Curta packed a sophisticated stepped-drum mechanism into a small cylinder, making it unusually portable for a mechanical calculator.
hearing aid — A hearing aid's gain is programmed from an audiogram, and probe-tube real-ear measurement can verify the sound delivered during fitting.
prosthetic limb — Prosthetic limbs may be passive, body-powered or myoelectric, and designs can be tailored to everyday use, sport or a particular occupation.
dialysis machine — A dialysis machine circulates blood through a dialyser, where diffusion and filtration remove substances the kidneys would normally clear.
cochlear implant — A cochlear implant combines an external sound processor with an internal electrode array that stimulates the auditory nerve.
artificial heart — An artificial heart replaces the heart's pumping action; a ventricular assist device supports one or both ventricles without replacing the whole heart.
Newton's cradle — Newton's cradle demonstrates how momentum and energy pass through a line of nearly elastic collisions, although the familiar desk toy dates from the 20th century.
Tesla coil — A Tesla coil is a resonant transformer circuit that produces very high-voltage alternating current and is often used for educational electrical displays.
Van de Graaff generator — A Van de Graaff generator accumulates static electric charge on a hollow metal globe, creating the high voltage behind the familiar hair-raising demonstration.
Rube Goldberg machine — Rube Goldberg drew cartoons of needlessly complicated inventions, and his name became an adjective for devices that reach a simple result through many indirect steps.
Crookes radiometer — A Crookes radiometer has light and dark vane faces inside a low-pressure bulb; heating the gas near the dark sides helps drive the rotation.
Y2K problem — Many older systems stored years with only two digits, so the change to 2000 risked bad comparisons and calculations; extensive remediation limited the disruption.
ILOVEYOU worm — ILOVEYOU arrived as a Visual Basic script disguised as a text file and used the victim's address book to send further copies.
Heartbleed — Heartbleed abused malformed heartbeat requests to read beyond the intended buffer, potentially exposing passwords and cryptographic material.
Pentium FDIV bug — The Pentium FDIV bug came from missing entries in a lookup table used by the processor's floating-point division algorithm.
Zune 30 freeze — The Zune 30's internal clock driver mishandled the final day of the 2008 leap year, and the players recovered automatically after 24 hours.
Google Glass — Google Glass displayed information through an optical head-mounted display and could record images, but the consumer version never became a mainstream wearable.
Segway PT — The Segway PT used gyroscopes and electric motors to balance a standing rider, but sales fell far short of the extraordinary launch hype.
Nokia N-Gage — The N-Gage combined a mobile phone with cartridge-based gaming, but its awkward first design struggled against dedicated handheld consoles.
HD DVD — HD DVD and Blu-ray competed to replace DVD for high-definition video; Toshiba ended the HD DVD business after studios and retailers shifted toward Blu-ray.
Sinclair C5 — The Sinclair C5 was a small electric recumbent tricycle sold as personal transport, but it disappeared from the market within months.
Deep Blue — Deep Blue won the six-game rematch 3½–2½, becoming the first computer to defeat a reigning world chess champion in a match under standard conditions.
AlphaGo — AlphaGo combined neural networks with tree search and defeated one of the world's strongest Go players in a landmark match.
IBM Watson — IBM Watson analysed natural-language clues, generated candidate answers and assigned confidence scores quickly enough to compete through the show's buzzer.
Libratus — Libratus used game-theory methods to improve its poker strategy and decisively beat four professional players in a 2017 competition.
TD-Gammon — TD-Gammon became an influential reinforcement-learning example because it discovered strong backgammon play largely through experience rather than an expert-written strategy book.
404 Not Found — HTTP status 404 means the server was reached but could not find the requested resource; it does not necessarily mean the whole website is offline.
Clippy — Clippy was the default character for the Microsoft Office Assistant, which tried to infer a user's task and offer help.
Ctrl-Alt-Delete — Ctrl-Alt-Delete began as a quick way for IBM PC developers to reboot without cycling the power and later gained a separate Windows security role.
Konami Code — The Konami Code was left in Gradius and later appeared in many Konami games, becoming one of gaming's best-known cheat codes.
Hello, World! program — The Hello, World! example became a standard way to show the basic syntax needed to produce output in a new programming language.
Volkswagen Beetle — The Volkswagen Beetle paired its rounded body with an air-cooled rear engine and became one of history's most-produced car designs.
original Mini — The original Mini's transverse engine and front-wheel-drive layout saved so much space that the design influenced generations of compact cars.
Citroën DS — The Citroën DS used hydraulic pressure for its self-levelling suspension and became famous for both its ride and avant-garde styling.
Tucker 48 — Only 50 production cars were completed; counting the prototype, 51 Tucker cars were made before the company folded.
Tatra 77 — The Tatra 77 combined Hans Ledwinka's rear-engined chassis with a streamlined body developed with aerodynamicist Paul Jaray.
Furby — Furby used sensors and motorised movements to appear responsive; its programmed vocabulary gradually shifted from Furbish toward English phrases.
laser tag — Laser tag equipment usually sends coded infrared light from the gun to targets on an opponent's vest or equipment.
Nintendo Game & Watch — Each Game & Watch model contained a fixed LCD game and also worked as a clock, foreshadowing later Nintendo handhelds.
Simon electronic game — Simon presents a random sequence through its four large buttons, and each successful round adds another signal for the player to remember.
RoboSapien — RoboSapien was a remote-controlled walking robot toy by WowWee, designed by Mark Tilden and launched in 2004.
Windows 95 startup sound — Microsoft commissioned Brian Eno to create the Windows 95 startup piece, officially titled The Microsoft Sound.
Intel bong — The Intel sonic logo compressed the Intel Inside brand into five notes and became one of advertising's most recognisable audio signatures.
THX Deep Note — James A. Moorer created the THX Deep Note for the company's cinema trailers, using computer-generated voices that converge on a broad final chord.
Macintosh startup chime — The Macintosh startup chime signalled that the machine's diagnostic tests had completed successfully before the operating system loaded.
AOL “You've Got Mail” greeting — Edwards recorded AOL's familiar mail announcement on a cassette at home, and the phrase became a lasting symbol of dial-up internet culture.
cuckoo clock — A cuckoo clock marks the hours with a bird call, usually using bellows and pipes, and the carved wooden style became closely linked with the Black Forest.
Doomsday Clock — The Doomsday Clock is a metaphorical warning created by atomic scientists; its hands represent their assessment of global human-made threats.
quartz clock — A quartz clock uses the regular resonance of a crystal as its frequency reference, making accurate electronic timekeeping inexpensive and compact.
marine chronometer — A marine chronometer kept reliable reference time despite a ship's motion and changing conditions, allowing longitude to be calculated from the time difference.
Clock of the Long Now — The Clock of the Long Now is a mechanical monument intended to keep time for 10,000 years as a symbol of long-term responsibility.
Rickrolling — The bait-and-switch joke disguises the destination of a link, then redirects the victim to Astley's music video.
Numa Numa video — Brolsma recorded the energetic lip-sync at his desk and uploaded it in 2004, helping define the early viral-video era.
Dancing Baby — The computer animation circulated by email and websites before its television appearance made it even more widely known.
Hampster Dance — The historical Hampster spelling came from the page's name; its looping GIFs and squeaky music made it an early internet phenomenon.
All Your Base meme — The awkward translation came from Zero Wing and became one of the best-known catchphrases of early internet culture.

assertion: original Ferris Wheel — Engineer George Washington Gale Ferris Jr designed the wheel for the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
moving walkway — The 1893 fair's looped passenger conveyor is described as the first moving walkway and included standing and seated platforms.
Ford Mustang — The Mustang made its public debut at Ford's pavilion at the 1964 fair before becoming the model that defined the pony-car class.
Picturephone — Picturephone was the Bell System and later AT&T brand for its videophone products and demonstrations.
Unisphere — The Unisphere was built as the fair's theme symbol and remains in Flushing Meadows–Corona Park.
cat's eye road stud — Shaw's reflector sends light back toward its source, helping drivers follow road markings in darkness.
sharkskin swimsuit — Fairhurst led the design of Speedo's Fastskin suit, whose surface drew on the ridged texture of shark skin.
lotus-effect coating — The lotus effect combines a water-repellent surface with microscopic roughness so droplets collect contaminants as they roll off.
gecko-inspired adhesive — Artificial setae reproduce the attachment principle of gecko toes and can be arranged into reusable dry adhesive surfaces.
Mercedes-Benz Bionic — Mercedes-Benz used the boxfish as the biological model for the Bionic concept's aerodynamics and lightweight construction.
first website — The first website was created by Berners-Lee at CERN in August 1991, the same month his WorldWideWeb browser became publicly available.
Million Dollar Homepage — Alex Tew launched the page to raise money for university, selling its million-pixel advertising grid in small blocks.
broken laser pointer — Omidyar contacted the buyer to confirm the sale was intentional and learned that he collected broken laser pointers.
AT&T's HotWired banner ad — HotWired put the AT&T banner online on 27 October 1994. It was the first web banner sold by HotWired, though other early-banner claims exist.
Les Horribles Cernettes — The CERN parody band appeared in a backstage photograph that became the first band photo published on the World Wide Web.
Nintendo Game Boy — The Game Boy paired durable portable hardware with interchangeable cartridges, and Tetris helped broaden its audience.
Wii Remote — The controller combined motion sensing with pointing functions and became the Wii console's defining interface.
Kinect — Kinect used cameras, depth sensing and microphones to interpret body movement and voice for Xbox systems.
Oculus Rift — Oculus VR launched the Rift's Kickstarter in 2012; the $300 DK1 helped developers prepare for the line's eventual consumer release.
Nintendo Virtual Boy — The Virtual Boy used a red stereoscopic display but was discontinued after a brief and unsuccessful market life.
Wikipedia — Its wiki model let contributors edit articles directly, in contrast with Nupedia's slower expert-review process.
Linux — Torvalds later switched the kernel from its original licence to the GNU GPL, and contributors around the world developed it further.
Raspberry Pi — The Raspberry Pi Foundation designed the small computer to make programming and computing more accessible in education.
Arduino — Arduino combines openly documented microcontroller boards with software tools intended for accessible electronics projects.
GNU Project — GNU expands recursively to GNU's Not Unix and was launched to build a completely free Unix-compatible operating system.
Netflix Prize — The Netflix Prize challenged teams to predict user ratings more accurately than the company's existing Cinematch algorithm.
Millennium Technology Prize — The Finnish award honours technological innovations that improve people's quality of life and promote sustainable development.
Ansari X Prize — The prize rewarded the first privately financed reusable crewed spacecraft to complete the required two flights.
DARPA Grand Challenge — The first event ended without a finisher, while later challenges demonstrated rapid progress in driverless navigation.
Orteig Prize — Hotel owner Raymond Orteig offered the prize for the first nonstop flight between New York and Paris.
Spot robot — Spot is a mobile quadruped designed to cross terrain that was difficult for earlier robots; it has also performed inspection work at hazardous sites.
ASIMO — Honda developed ASIMO as a research humanoid capable of increasingly natural bipedal movement and interaction.
Aibo — Aibo was designed as an autonomous entertainment robot with dog-like movement and behaviour rather than as a working machine.
Unimate — Unimate became the first industrial robot installed on a production line, handling hot die-cast parts at General Motors.
Shakey the robot — Shakey used cameras and sensors with planning software so it could reason about a sequence of actions in its environment.
